stops.title: The Cascadia Subduction Zone
stops.narration: Off the coast of the Pacific Northwest, the Juan de Fuca plate is diving beneath North America at roughly 40 mm per year. This 1,100 km long boundary — from Cape Mendocino to Vancouver Island — is one of Earth's most dangerous seismic zones.

stops.title: The Diving Plate
stops.narration: Seismic data reveals the subducting slab's geometry. It descends gently at first, then steepens to nearly 45 degrees as it plunges toward the mantle. This slab geometry controls where earthquakes occur and where magma rises to feed the Cascade volcanoes.

stops.title: Ring of Fire
stops.narration: The Cascade volcanic arc sits directly above where the slab reaches 80–100 km depth — the depth at which dehydration melting produces magma. Mount Rainier, St. Helens, Hood, and Baker are all products of this process.

stops.title: Locked and Loading
stops.narration: GPS stations across the Pacific Northwest show the continent being compressed eastward — pushed by the diving plate. Where the fault is fully locked (shown in red), strain accumulates year after year. When it releases, the result is a magnitude 9 earthquake.

stops.title: A Plate Tearing Apart
stops.narration: The Juan de Fuca plate isn't monolithic — it's fragmenting. A 35 km fracture has been discovered in the Explorer segment, and a new 'incipient tear' is forming further south. This gradual disintegration has been occurring for millions of years.

stops.title: The Lost Plate Fragment
stops.narration: In 2026, scientists discovered a hidden fragment of an ancient plate still moving beneath Northern California — right where the San Andreas Fault meets Cascadia. This 'Pioneer Fragment' suggests the two fault systems may be seismically coupled.

stops.title: When It Breaks
stops.narration: Computer simulations of a magnitude 9.0 Cascadia earthquake show violent shaking across the entire Pacific Northwest. The USGS has modeled 30 different rupture scenarios — each producing different patterns of devastation.

stops.title: The Wave That Follows
stops.narration: Within minutes of the earthquake, a tsunami would race across the Pacific. Coastal communities from Vancouver Island to Northern California could see waves exceeding 10 meters. The last time this happened was January 26, 1700.

stops.title: Watching and Waiting
stops.narration: A growing network of sensors — from seafloor observatories to GPS stations to DART buoys — monitors the subduction zone around the clock. But the vast majority of the locked fault lies offshore, beyond our best instruments. We know it will happen. We just don't know when.
